deep.reconstruction:
There are no derivations on this page. It is a page of philosophical and methodological notes, probably from about 1912–1913. That dating rests on the previous page quoting Einstein's letter to Sommerfeld of 29.10.1912 and on the references to Planck's 'Acht Vorlesungen über theoretische Physik' (1910) and 'Die Einheit des physikalischen Weltbildes' (1909). The page has five units.

(1) Top margin, continuing from the previous page: a reference 'vgl. Planck 8 Vorl. über theor. Physik S. 5–8 etc.' The sentence then ends: '...der spezifischen Sinnesempfindungen.' Hilbert adds that the higher development of logic, meaning pure epistemology, must consist in freeing it from anthropomorphic thinking ('our understanding in a certain sense'). This mirrors Planck's thesis that physics progresses by de-anthropomorphising its world picture.

(2) The 'Oberfrage' remark. For some problems the meta-question, presumably whether the problem can be solved or decided at all, is most easily answered by actually solving the problem.
- Example 1: show that p − q = 2 has infinitely many solutions in primes p, q. This is the twin prime conjecture, already named in Hilbert's 8th Paris problem of 1900. Here the solvability question would most likely only be settled by a proof or disproof.
- Example 2, the converse ('umgekehrt'): state the 10^(10^10)-th decimal digit of π. Here the meta-question is trivial. The digit exists and is computable by a finite algorithm, so the problem is solvable in principle. Yet actually producing the digit is practically out of reach.
- In modern terms, Hilbert separates decidability or solvability in principle from actually carrying out the solution, i.e. from feasibility.

(3) 'Philosophical theory of experimenting.' 'To have sense' (Sinn haben) means to obtain this or that as 'yes' or 'no' by mechanical experimenting. This is a proto-operational, decision-procedure criterion of meaningfulness.
- Applied to relativity: two definitions of time, i.e. two times, are perfectly possible, just as two geometries are. It makes no sense to say there is only one time or only one space.
- Hilbert then suggests it may likewise turn out to make no sense to say that there are unsolvable problems. This is his 'no ignorabimus' conviction, here grounded in a meaning criterion.

(4) The axiomatic method is especially appropriate in physics. It suits even subjects still 'in flux', as it does wherever concepts need clarifying. Compare Paris problem 6 of 1900 and Hilbert's physics lectures and foundations of physics of 1905–1915.

(5) Every physical theory, or theoretical consideration, must be qualitatively correct exactly as 2·2 = 4 is correct.

The only mathematics involved is the two example problems in (2).
errors: No mathematical errors. Classing the twin prime question as one whose solvability is probably only settled by solving it is a heuristic opinion, not a claim. Calling the π-digit problem the converse is correct: it is decidable in principle but practically infeasible.

results.what: Distinction between a problem's meta-question (is it solvable or decidable?) and solving it. Twin primes are given as a case where the meta-question probably needs the full solution; the 10^(10^10)-th digit of π as a case where solvability is trivial but execution is infeasible.
results.modern_name: Decidability/solvability in principle versus feasibility; an early large-index π-digit example of the kind used in the Brouwer/Hilbert debates
results.usually_credited_to: The twin prime problem was posed in Hilbert's 8th Paris problem (1900; earlier de Polignac 1849). π-digit examples are associated with Brouwer (1908 onward) and later with Hilbert/Bernays and Wittgenstein. Feasibility versus decidability comes from later complexity theory (1960s).

results.what: Meaningfulness criterion: 'Sinn haben' = obtainable as yes/no by mechanical experimenting. Hence perhaps 'there are unsolvable problems' has no sense.
results.modern_name: Operationalist or verificationist meaning criterion; decision procedure; precursor of the Entscheidungsproblem and of 'no ignorabimus'
results.usually_credited_to: No ignorabimus: Hilbert (1900, 1930). Operationalism: Bridgman (1927). Verificationism: Vienna Circle (1920s). Entscheidungsproblem: Hilbert–Ackermann (1928), Behmann (1921).

results.what: Plurality of time definitions in relativity, compared with the plurality of geometries; 'only one time/space' is said to be meaningless
The axiomatic method is appropriate in physics, including for theories still in flux

deep.surprise_reason: Most of the content consists of familiar Hilbertian themes from about 1912–13: no ignorabimus, the axiomatisation of physics, and Planck-style de-anthropomorphisation. Mildly notable is the explicit pairing of twin primes with the 10^(10^10)-th digit of π, which separates solvability in principle from actual execution. Also notable is a 'mechanical experimenting yields yes/no' meaning criterion that predates his formal decision-problem programme by some 15 years. These are interesting unpublished details, not new results.

checkable.sympy: [(p, p+2) for p in primerange(2, 100) if isprime(p+2)]
checkable.asserts: Small solutions of p - q = 2 in primes exist: (3,5), (5,7), (11,13), ... These illustrate the twin prime problem but do not settle whether there are infinitely many.

checkable.sympy: all((p+1) % 6 == 0 for p in primerange(5, 10000) if isprime(p+2))
checkable.asserts: Every twin pair beyond (3,5) has the form (6k-1, 6k+1). This is a routine property of the problem mentioned.
Decimal digits of π are computable by a finite procedure, so the n-th digit problem is decidable in principle. The 10^(10^10)-th digit is nonetheless far beyond feasible computation.
The digit index 10^(10^10) has 10^10 + 1 decimal digits itself.
